title: Structuring Digital Assets: Trusts, Entities and Access Plans for Crypto
summary: How wills, trusts, business entities and multisig access plans fit together to protect crypto and other digital assets during your life and pass them on after it.
body:
Most estate plans were written for a house, a bank account and a retirement fund. If you hold cryptocurrency, tokenized assets, an online business or digital content, those traditional documents may not reach them. And if no one can access your keys, those assets can be lost for good.

This article explains the main building blocks for structuring digital assets in Tennessee. It is general information, not legal advice for your situation.

## Why digital assets need their own plan

With a bank account, a court order and a death certificate usually get your family access. With self-custodied crypto, access depends on who controls the private keys or recovery phrase, and no court can recover a key that is lost. At the same time, sharing your recovery phrase today hands over full control today. A good plan solves both problems: the right people can reach your assets when it matters, and no one can reach them before then.

## Will or trust: the starting point

A will says who receives your property after you die and names the person who will manage your estate. It generally goes through probate, the court-supervised process for settling an estate, and probate filings can become public. Never put keys or recovery phrases in a will.

A revocable living trust is created while you are alive. You transfer assets into it, usually serve as your own trustee, and name a successor trustee to step in if you become incapacitated or die. Assets properly held in the trust can often pass without probate, and the trust terms stay private. A trust can also set out how and when beneficiaries receive assets, which matters when the assets are volatile or the beneficiaries are young.

For many people with significant digital assets, a trust paired with a short pour-over will is the core of the plan. The will catches anything left outside the trust.

## Holding digital assets in an entity

Some people hold crypto, tokenized real estate or an online business through a limited liability company. An LLC can:

- Keep business assets separate from personal ones.
- Make transfers simpler, since you transfer membership interests rather than individual assets.
- Spell out in its operating agreement who manages the assets if you cannot.

Your trust can then own the LLC, so the whole structure passes according to your plan.

## Access plans: multisig and instructions

Legal authority is only half the plan. Your representative also needs a secure, practical way in. Common tools include:

- Multisignature wallets: several keys exist, and more than one is needed to move funds. You might hold one key, a trusted person or professional custodian another, and keep a third in secure storage. No single person can take the assets, yet the plan still works if you are gone.
- A letter of instruction: a separate, private document describing what you own, where it is held and how to reach it, without writing keys out in the open.
- Exchange accounts: checking each platform's rules for death and incapacity, and making sure your documents give your representatives authority to deal with it.

## Authority for your representatives

Tennessee has a law addressing when executors, trustees and agents can access a person's digital accounts and records. In general, that access depends on what your documents say and on the platform's own terms. A durable power of attorney and your trust should expressly grant authority over digital assets, so the people you choose are not left arguing with a platform's support desk.

## Tennessee tools for larger plans

Tennessee law offers structures that can help when digital assets are a large part of what you own, such as trusts designed to last for generations and certain asset protection trusts. They must be set up correctly and in advance, and they are not right for everyone.

## Taxes

The IRS generally treats digital assets as property. How assets are held during life and how they pass at death can affect the tax basis your heirs receive. Tennessee does not currently have a state inheritance or estate tax, but federal rules apply and tax laws can change.

## Keep the plan current

Digital portfolios change quickly: new wallets, new platforms, new kinds of assets. Review your plan when you add a new type of asset, change how you hold your keys, marry, have children or start a business.
